extracted.intended_audience: college faculty, curriculum designers, and administrators responsible for general education and quantitative reasoning programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, running, and assessing undergraduate quantitative reasoning (QR) basic-skills and applied-skills courses and QR projects embedded across disciplines. Covers learning goals, project requirements, pedagogical design, and assessment metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR Basic Skills Requirement — expected content
rubrics_metrics.description: A student who has satisfied the QR basic skills requirement will demonstrate a baseline understanding of such topics as algebra, graphing, geometry, data analysis, and linearity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course (Mathematics 100 example) should include weekly computer lab work (Excel) to graph data, analyze data, explore and model growth, and learn about loans and financial planning. Emphasize mathematical and statistical reasoning and use of appropriate tools for summarizing data, making predictions, and establishing cause-and-effect relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals of the QR Basic Skills Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand mathematical and statistical reasoning; to use appropriate mathematical and/or statistical tools in summarizing data, making predictions, and establishing cause-and-effect relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course design should build conceptual understanding and practical tool use (e.g., spreadsheets) rather than rote manipulative skill alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR Applied Skills Requirement — purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The QR applied skills requirement is designed to provide students with the opportunity to apply quantitative skills as they solve problems in fields of study in which they have an interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied QR should let students apply quantitative/statistical reasoning within disciplinary contexts; projects must advance course goals and not be merely rote procedure-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR Applied Course minimal structural requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each QR applied course must include at least two QR projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application form for course approval requires instructors to describe the two QR projects so reviewers can ascertain that proposed projects fit guidelines. Reviewers may ask for clarification or revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible activities within a QR project
rubrics_metrics.description: A project might include data collection, discussion of the data, collaborative work on finding appropriate uses of the data, and use of appropriate technology in presentation and writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should incorporate active data work, group interaction, and appropriate technical tools (e.g., Excel) with presentation/written components.

rubrics_metrics.name: QR project final deliverable requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The end result of each QR project should be a written assignment that includes a statement of the problem, an explanation of the methods used, and a summary of the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, the written assignment should discuss any limitations encountered and possible improvements to the procedure and/or results. In some disciplines treat the write-up as a technical report combining prose and mathematics/figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project design pedagogy — stepwise, scaffolded tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Many assignments are multi-step procedures involving data collection, calculation, presentation of the results, and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step-by-step structure alleviates student anxiety, makes assignments accessible, and fits naturally in course material. Scaffolding (e.g., do first wash together, subsequent washes individually) and peer review are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real-life, messy data
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative reasoning exercises should come from real-life examples and data rather than contrived textbook examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real data invites struggle, ownership, and deeper interpretation; exposes students to data limitations and ambiguity, which supports authentic understanding and interdisciplinary connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative/group work as an instructional feature
rubrics_metrics.description: Group work, especially for data collection, was a common feature and faculty found that students enjoyed working with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design projects to allow students to contribute different strengths; group work can add fun, reduce stigma around QR, and improve class dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific project goals (history example)
rubrics_metrics.description: History QR project goals include encouraging students to think about changes over time in family life, learning vocabulary distinguishing family types, exposing students to varieties and limits of historical data, and exercising quantitative skills (mean, median, mode; creating tables/graphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects in non-math disciplines should combine disciplinary concepts (vocabulary, interpretation) with explicit practice of basic quantitative operations and data representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific project goals (classics/ancient art example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce textual and material evidence, teach quantitative skills necessary for deeper understanding (e.g., ratios of column height to diameter), graphing trends, reconstructing plans from fragmentary data, and using modular scaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate measurement, unit/scale choices, and graphical analysis that an active practitioner in the discipline would use; encourage questions raised by gaps in the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project requirement: technical report and interpretation (calculus/law example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must present both the mathematical work and a verbal argument (technical report) giving their verdict (e.g., on liability in the McDonald’s coffee lawsuit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame assignments as technical reports combining writing and calculations; require discussion of model assumptions, error margins (e.g., 'if plaintiff was off by x seconds'), and interpretive reasoning linking math to real-world judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical data-collection and fieldwork expectations (ecology example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects should include hands-on data collection (pairs), summarization (life tables), drawing survivorship curves, and use of appropriate graphing techniques (e.g., semilog graphs); background readings and lab prep are expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure students are prepared with necessary methods/Excel skills before fieldwork; aggregate and summarize class-collected data for further analysis and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for numerical and prose conclusions and reflection (history/Napoleon example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Student papers must include an explanation of the mathematical processes, present conclusions both numerically and in prose, analyze results, and discuss what they learned (including qualitative descriptors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect reflective components that connect quantitative results to historical or domain understanding; prompt students to state adjectives/qualitative judgments where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-to-practice translation (lighting design example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Project goals: create a light plot that includes three washes for a bare stage; choose correct instrumentation; determine best placement of instruments for continuity of angle of light; break down stage space into scaled/ sized areas and prepare ground plans/section views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use progressive assignments to build competency (group-first then individual), use physical lab space when possible, and teach scale/module systems to simplify fractional measurements—emphasize technical paperwork and systematic planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment instruments and metrics for program effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment uses final course grades (pass rates, average quality points), a pre/post quantitative reasoning assessment (50-point test with average improvement reported), and student perception surveys (percent change on survey items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track multiple measures: administrative outcome data (grades/pass rates), objective pre/post test gains (report raw and percent improvement), and qualitative/self-report measures. Participate in instrument-development efforts (e.g., NSF projects) to refine assessment tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty development and review process for QR courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty workshops, peer review of QR assignments, and a screening/approval committee process (application form describing projects) are used to develop and vet QR applied courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide faculty with templates and opportunities to test assignments in workshops; peer feedback helps refine projects and broaden cross-disciplinary buy-in. Screening committees should request clarifications and revisions to ensure fit with QR guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-level learning outcomes and broader aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide students with knowledge, ability, and confidence to solve and understand quantitative issues; prepare informed citizens who can interpret numerical information in public life; and give skills valued by employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curriculum and projects to foster transferable problem-solving skills, interpretive judgment, and confidence with numbers across disciplines; emphasize application beyond the classroom.
